The activation of BAT through the adrenergic sympathetic pathway was ﬁrst studied in rodents. Three b-adrenergic receptors were
identiﬁed: b1-AR, b2-AR and b3-AR. Stimulation of b3-AR was found to increase energy expenditure in mice (Berbée et al., 2015),
although b3-AR agonists failed to produce clinical effects on weight loss in humans. As these studies were performed before the
development of 18F-FDG PET/CT imaging, it was unclear if b3-AR agonists were capable of stimulating BAT in humans. Interest
in b3-AR agonists reignited in 2015, when the new b3-AR agonist mirabegron was approved to treat overactive bladder. Stimulation
with mirabegron was found to increase lipid oxidation, supraclavicular skin temperature and a decrease in BAT fat fraction and an
increase in BAT activity as measured by 18F-FDG PET/CT. However, there were also reports of unwanted cardiovascular responses,
which led to the suspicion that high doses of mirabegron were not selective to the b3-AR, and that the responses were the result of
general b-AR stimulation. This hypothesis was proven to be correct when a high dose of mirabegron was found to increase heart rate
and WAT lipolysis, which are b1- and b2- AR-dependent responses. Furthermore, the activation of BAT was found to rely on stim-
ulation of b2-AR. In vitro stimulation of brown adipocytes with the highly selective b2-AR agonist formoterol increased uncoupled
respiration, while the b3-AR agonist mirabegron had no such effect (Blondin et al., 2020). The previously reported clinical results of
